mcqs.question: According to the performance equation (Time = Instructions x CPI x Clock period), which of the following could make a lower-clocked CPU finish a task faster than a higher-clocked one?
options: It's impossible — a higher clock speed always wins
A sufficiently lower CPI or fewer required instructions, outweighing the clock period difference
Only if the lower-clocked CPU has more cache
Only if both CPUs use the exact same ISA
mcqs.explanation: Since execution time is the product of all three terms, a big enough advantage in CPI or instruction count can overcome a clock-period disadvantage entirely — this is a direct algebraic consequence of the equation. Cache isn't one of the three terms directly, and the equation applies regardless of whether the two CPUs share an ISA.

mcqs.question: Why is comparing two different ISAs' performance using raw MIPS (millions of instructions per second) misleading?
options: MIPS can only be measured on RISC processors
An instruction on one ISA (e.g. a rich CISC instruction) may accomplish far more work than an instruction on another (e.g. a simple RISC instruction), so equal MIPS doesn't mean equal work done
MIPS is always identical to clock speed in GHz
MIPS cannot be measured for floating-point workloads
mcqs.explanation: The core flaw is that "an instruction" isn't a standard unit of work across ISAs — a single CISC instruction can do what several RISC instructions need, so raw instruction-count-per-second comparisons don't reflect actual work accomplished. MIPS can be measured on any ISA, isn't the same number as clock speed, and isn't restricted to integer workloads.

mcqs.question: Design A: 2.0B instructions, CPI 1.2, clock 3 GHz. Design B: 1.6B instructions, CPI 1.5, clock 3.5 GHz. Which finishes faster, and why?
options: Design A, because it has the lower CPI
Design B, because it needs fewer instructions and its faster clock more than compensates for its higher CPI
They finish in exactly the same time
Design A, because CPI is the only term that matters
mcqs.explanation: Time_A = 2.0e9 x 1.2 / 3.0e9 = 0.80s; Time_B = 1.6e9 x 1.5 / 3.5e9 ~= 0.686s. B wins despite the higher CPI because its lower instruction count and faster clock period dominate the product. No single term (CPI alone) determines the winner.

mcqs.question: What is "benchmarketing", and why does it undermine trusting a benchmark score directly for your own workload?
options: It's a marketing term with no technical meaning
Tuning hardware or compilers specifically to excel at a well-known benchmark's exact code paths, without that tuning generalizing to other software
Running a benchmark suite on multiple different CPUs simultaneously
A benchmark methodology that only measures marketing department efficiency
mcqs.explanation: Benchmarketing describes over-fitting a system to a specific, well-known benchmark rather than to real-world performance broadly — meaning a top score there doesn't guarantee it'll be fastest for a different workload the benchmark didn't specifically target.
